hints: Think of a relay as two separate parts - a low-voltage electromagnet coil that is powered by the op-amp, and a separate high-voltage switch that turns the lamp on. Where must the coil get its current from?
The coil needs a complete loop from the op-amp output back to 0 V, and the lamp needs its own mains loop to be closed by the relay switch. Trace the two pairs of terminals on the right of Fig. 9.1.
walkthrough:
**Separate the Two Sides of a Relay**
You sitting beside me, remember a relay keeps the delicate electronics safe from the mains. The coil is the input side driven by the op-amp. The reed switch is the output side in series with the lamp and its a.c. supply. They are magnetically linked but electrically isolated.

**Complete Both Loops**
Connect the coil between the terminal after the diode and the earthed terminal. This lets current from the op-amp circuit flow through the coil back to earth. Connect the normally-open relay contacts between the two terminals of the lamp circuit on the far right, so when the coil is energised the switch closes and current flows through the lamp to light it.

Final answer: Connect the relay coil between the diode output terminal and the earth (0 V) terminal. Connect the relay switch contacts across the lamp circuit terminals so the lamp, mains supply and switch are in series.

hints: For the lamp to light, current must flow through the relay coil to energise it. Look carefully at which way the diode triangle points - which direction can conventional current pass through it?
Compare the voltage at the earthed end of the coil (0 V) with the voltage needed at the op-amp end to push current through the forward-biased diode and into or out of the op-amp.
walkthrough:
**Check the Diode Direction**
The diode in Fig. 9.1 only allows conventional current to flow leftwards, towards the op-amp output. It blocks current flowing rightwards out of the op-amp. So to energise the coil, current must come from earth, go through the coil from right to left, then through the diode into the op-amp.

**Why the Output Must Be Negative**
That current direction is only possible if the op-amp end is at a lower potential than the earth end. The op-amp must saturate at about $-5\text{ V}$. The diode is forward biased with about $0.7\text{ V}$ across it, the coil is energised, the relay switch closes and the lamp is switched on. A positive output would reverse bias the diode, so no coil current flows.

Final answer: Output is negative, about -5 V saturation. The diode is then forward biased so current flows from earth through the relay coil and through the diode into the op-amp output, energising the coil to close the lamp switch.

hints: Which sensor is made as a thin wire grid whose resistance changes when it is stretched or compressed with the object it is glued to?
walkthrough:
**Link Bending to Resistance**
When a rod bends, its surface stretches or compresses. A strain gauge glued to the rod stretches with it, its wire becomes longer and thinner so its resistance increases. Placed in the potential divider in Fig. 9.1, this changes $V-$ or $V+$ and flips the comparator to indicate the bending.

hints: Which sensor has a resistance that falls in bright light and rises in the dark, ideal for detecting daylight level?
walkthrough:
**Link Light Level to Resistance**
An LDR is the natural device for daylight detection. In daylight its resistance is low, in darkness its resistance is high. In the divider this gives a large voltage change between day and night, so the comparator output changes and the relay switches the street light on when it gets dark.
